blocks.text: A **number system** writes numerical values using digits and a fixed set of rules. The **base** (also called the **radix**) is the count of distinct digits the system uses, including zero. Computers work in binary, while people prefer decimal, so exams keep asking how to move between the two.

Conventional digital computers store data and machine instructions as **binary patterns**. One binary digit is one **bit**. The processor executes machine instructions directly, and those instructions are binary too.

blocks.title: Validity check: is this number legal?
items: **1010, 1111, 1001** and **0001** are valid binary patterns.
**1201** is not binary, because binary has no digit 2.
Octal has exactly eight symbols (0 to 7), so **8 and 9 are invalid** octal digits.
**BAD, BED, ACE** are valid hexadecimal numbers; **BEG** is not, because G lies outside A to F.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: The biggest digit in any system is always one less than its base: binary 1, octal 7, decimal 9, hex F (which equals 15).

A digit's value depends on **where it sits**. Starting at the rightmost whole-number digit, the positions carry weights of base⁰, base¹, base², and so on. That is why 5 in 50 is worth more than 5 in 5.
The small subscript tells you the base. The same digits mean different values in different bases, so always label the base in your answer.

blocks.title: Data units build up
items: Bit
0 or 1
Nibble
4 bits
Byte
8 bits = 2 nibbles
KiB
1024 bytes

blocks.title: KB or KiB?
blocks.text: Older exam material often calls 1024 bytes '1 KB'. The precise name for 1024 bytes is **KiB**, while kB (kilobyte) strictly means 1000 bytes in decimal notation.

sections.title: BCD, ASCII, Parity and Why Octal and Hex

blocks.title: Important codes
rows: Binary-Coded Decimal; standard 8421 BCD gives each decimal digit its own 4-bit group
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
7 bits, so 128 code values (0 to 127): letters, digits, punctuation and control codes
Several 8-bit extensions with up to 256 values; their character mappings differ

blocks.text: BCD example: decimal **59** becomes **0101 1001**, because 5 is 0101 and 9 is 1001. Each digit is encoded separately, so BCD is not the same as converting the whole number to binary.

blocks.title: Parity bit
rows: Total number of 1s (data plus parity bit) is even
Total number of 1s (data plus parity bit) is odd

blocks.title: What parity can and cannot do
blocks.text: A parity bit helps **detect** certain errors in transmission or storage. A single parity bit detects an odd number of bit flips; it cannot detect every error and cannot correct errors by itself.

blocks.title: Why use octal and hexadecimal?
items: **Octal** shortens binary: one octal digit equals 3 bits.
**Hexadecimal** is common in programming, debugging and memory-address displays: one hex digit equals 4 bits.
The underlying data always remains binary; octal and hex are only shorter ways to write it.

blocks.title: Binary to decimal
items: Write the weight of each position under the bits: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (rightmost bit has weight 2⁰ = 1).
Multiply every bit by its weight.
Add all the contributions.

blocks.title: Decimal to binary (sum of powers of 2)
items: Break the number into a sum of powers of 2.
Write 1 under every weight you used and 0 under every weight you skipped.
Read the bits from the highest weight to the lowest.

blocks.title: Alternative: repeated division by 2, shown for 25

blocks.text: Read the remainders from **bottom to top**: 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, so (25)₁₀ = (11001)₂, matching the first method. Leading zeros do not change an unsigned value, and you should always label the base.
Because 8 = 2³, **one octal digit equals exactly three bits**. This makes octal a compact way to write long binary patterns.

blocks.title: Octal to binary
items: Replace every octal digit with exactly three bits.
Keep the zeros inside each group.
Join the groups; leading zeros of the whole answer may be dropped.

blocks.title: Binary to octal
items: Group the whole-number bits in threes, starting from the right.
Pad the leftmost group with zeros if it has fewer than three bits.
Convert each group to one octal digit.

blocks.text: Since 16 = 2⁴, **one hex digit equals four bits**. The letters A to F stand for the decimal values 10 to 15.

blocks.title: Binary to hex
items: Group the bits in fours, starting from the right.
Pad the left with zeros to complete the last group.
Replace each group with its hex digit.

blocks.text: Octal groups of 3 bits, hex groups of 4 bits. Remember '8 = 2³ so 3, 16 = 2⁴ so 4'.

Work from **right to left** and include any incoming carry. Example: (1010)₂ + (0011)₂ = (1101)₂, and the decimal check agrees: 10 + 3 = 13. Digital logic circuits in the processor carry out binary arithmetic.

blocks.title: Subtraction rules
rows: Borrow from the next higher position; the borrowed 1 becomes two units, so (10)₂ − (1)₂ = (1)₂

blocks.title: Worked subtraction examples (align the rightmost digits, pad with leading zeros)

blocks.text: Binary 1 + 1 is **10** (read 'one zero'), not decimal ten. Binary 1 + 1 + 1 is **11**, not decimal eleven.

The **binary point** separates the whole part from the fractional part. To its left are non-negative powers of 2; to its right are negative powers of 2. To convert, multiply each bit by its positional weight and add the results.
The first place after the binary point is worth **one-half (0.5)**, not one-tenth.

Complements change a digit pattern by a fixed rule. They help implement subtraction, signed-number representation and logical operations. Always fix the **bit length first**, because leading zeros turn into ones and different widths give different answers.

blocks.title: One's complement
rows: Invert every bit (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0) and keep exactly the original length

blocks.title: Notation matters
blocks.text: If '10' means the two-bit binary pattern (10)₂, its one's complement is 01. If it means decimal 10 in four bits, the pattern is 1010 and the complement is 0101. State the width first.

blocks.title: Finding the two's complement
items: Fix the bit length
Choose the width first
Invert every bit
This gives the one's complement
Add 1 at the LSB
LSB is the rightmost bit
Keep the width
Discard any carry beyond it

blocks.text: Two's complement is widely used for **signed integers**: it represents positive values, zero and negative values, and is especially handy for encoding negative integers. Subtraction can be done by adding the two's complement of the number being subtracted, at a fixed width. Two's complement equals one's complement plus 1, and never change the width halfway through the calculation.

blocks.title: Rules
items: **Nine's complement**: subtract each decimal digit from 9. For n digits it is (10ⁿ − 1) − N, so use as many 9s as the chosen digit length.
**Ten's complement**: nine's complement plus 1. For a nonzero N in n digits it equals 10ⁿ − N.
Choose the digit length first and keep it fixed; discard overflow beyond that width.
The fixed-width ten's complement of zero is zero.

blocks.text: To show the ten's complement of 28 in BCD, encode 72 digit by digit: 7 = 0111 and 2 = 0010, so the BCD result is **0111 0010**. That is decimal ten's complement followed by BCD encoding.
Nine's complement is a digit-by-digit 'subtract from 9'. Ten's complement is just one more: add 1.
Standard **8421 BCD** encodes each decimal digit separately using four bits weighted 8, 4, 2, 1. The groups 0000 to 1001 are valid; 1010 to 1111 are not valid decimal-digit groups.

blocks.title: BCD to ordinary binary
items: Split the BCD into four-bit groups.
Decode each group as one decimal digit.
Combine the digits into a decimal number.
Convert that whole decimal value to ordinary binary.

blocks.text: BCD 0010 1000 and binary 11100 both stand for decimal 28, but they follow different encoding rules. Always distinguish the base, the encoding and the bit width.

revision: Bases: binary 2, octal 8, decimal 10, hexadecimal 16; the base counts the distinct digits including zero.
Binary digits are 0 and 1, octal 0 to 7, decimal 0 to 9, hex 0 to 9 and A to F; 1201 is invalid binary, 8 and 9 are invalid octal, BEG is invalid hex.
Nibble = 4 bits, byte = 8 bits = 2 nibbles; KiB = 1024 bytes (precise binary unit), kB = 1000 bytes.
BCD = Binary-Coded Decimal: each decimal digit gets its own 4-bit group (decimal 59 = 0101 1001).
Standard ASCII is 7 bits with 128 values (0 to 127); extended ASCII is 8-bit with up to 256 values.
A parity bit helps detect errors (even parity: even count of 1s; odd parity: odd count); it does not correct them.
One octal digit = 3 bits (8 = 2³); one hex digit = 4 bits (16 = 2⁴); hex D = 13; FF = 255.
Binary to decimal: multiply each bit by its weight (16, 8, 4, 2, 1) and add; decimal to binary: sum of powers of 2.
Binary addition: 1+1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1) and 1+1+1 = 11; example 1010 + 0011 = 1101, and 1101 − 0101 = 1000.
Binary fractions: first place after the point is 0.5; (0.1011)₂ = 0.6875 and (1101.1011)₂ = 13.6875.
One's complement: invert all bits at a fixed width; two's complement: invert all bits, then add 1 (LSB = rightmost bit).
Nine's complement: subtract each digit from 9 (28 → 71); ten's complement: nine's complement + 1 (28 → 72, 455 → 545).
8421 BCD groups 1010 to 1111 are invalid; BCD 1001 1000 = decimal 98 = binary 1100010.
Octal shortens long binary patterns; hex is common for memory-address displays; the underlying data stays binary.
